method.audio: Authorized low-resolution YouTube video downloaded with yt-dlp and converted to mono 16 kHz WAV.
method.review: Complete chronological ASR read by independent research agents; page and frame anchors were separately checked.
method.script_boundary: Public third-party screenplay copies are used only for page alignment and short locating phrases. They are not redistributed and may differ from the exact production draft.
method.interpretation_boundary: Video analysis remains E4 commentary. Sampled frames prove only visible anchors, not movement, sound, edit causality or filmmaker intent.

claims.paraphrase: The video frames Arrival as a chain of changes from Ted Chiang's story to Heisserer's screenplay and then to Villeneuve/Walker's film edit.
claims.uncertainty: Commentator framing; contribution boundaries require independent production evidence.

claims.paraphrase: The story's already-knowing narrator is reframed as a protagonist discovering the language, and future images are distributed so audience knowledge advances with Louise.
claims.uncertainty: Narrative interpretation; sampled stills cannot prove temporal order alone.

claims.paraphrase: The story's remote looking-glass communication becomes an arrival at Earth's door in the screenplay/film.
claims.uncertainty: Video frame and script page provide visible anchors; exact source-story wording is not distributed here.

claims.paraphrase: Face-to-face arrival is said to create immediate threat, public hysteria and institutional conflict sufficient for feature-length pressure.
claims.uncertainty: Causal sufficiency is commentary, not a controlled comparison.

claims.paraphrase: Hannah's death changes from an adult climbing accident in the story to an incurable disease during adolescence in the screenplay/film.
claims.uncertainty: The sampled video page shows age dialogue but not the full death-cause comparison.

claims.paraphrase: The video links the incurable illness to a more consequential free-will choice for Louise, who cannot prevent the loss she foresees.
claims.uncertainty: Interpretation of theme and choice; not verified by one page or frame.

claims.paraphrase: Heisserer describes a third version of the film emerging in editing through scene removal, compression and adjustment.
claims.uncertainty: Interview excerpt as presented by LFTS; the full interview context should be consulted for high-stakes attribution.

claims.paraphrase: Several separate screenplay explanations are said to move into a short mid-film montage and voiceover carrying nonlinear orthography, learning and naming information.
claims.uncertainty: Static frames show several source/film states but do not prove montage timing or exact voiceover placement.

claims.paraphrase: A screenplay section where Weber doubts Louise and temporarily replaces her is described as removed while preserving the needed Sapir-Whorf information elsewhere.
claims.uncertainty: Page anchors exist; the complete omission requires comparing the whole finished-film sequence.

claims.paraphrase: An accidental hard juxtaposition during editing is presented as inspiring a dreamlike psychological reconstruction of the sequence.
claims.uncertainty: Editorial causality comes from quoted production recollection and cannot be proved by stills.

claims.paraphrase: The line about dreaming in the alien language is described as transferred from a Weber exchange to a heptapod exchange using visual effects.
claims.uncertainty: Frames and pages anchor the elements but do not prove the exact replacement process.

claims.paraphrase: Omission and reordering are said to narrow the sequence around Louise's arc.
claims.uncertainty: Commentator conclusion; needs a competing explanation such as runtime or clarity.

claims.paraphrase: The circular, nonlinear alien script is presented as a formal mirror for questions about human linear language and time.
claims.uncertainty: Theme interpretation; visible logograms do not prove intended metaphor.

claims.paraphrase: Louise's patience and communication are contrasted with human fear, impatience and institutional silence; the video attributes much conflict to human response rather than alien aggression.
claims.uncertainty: Interpretive synthesis across selected scenes.

items.title: The Social Network — Sorkin, Structure, and Collaboration

claims.paraphrase: The video describes Sorkin's rapid, witty dialogue as a highly noticeable style.
claims.uncertainty: Critical description, not an objective quality metric.

claims.paraphrase: Verbal flash is interpreted as carrying substance without making the delivery feel expository.
claims.uncertainty: Commentator metaphor.

claims.paraphrase: The stated analysis separates dialogue style, nonlinear structure and collaboration as three craft layers.
claims.uncertainty: The video's organizing thesis.

claims.paraphrase: An interview excerpt presents Sorkin's experience of dialogue as music.
claims.uncertainty: Quoted interview excerpt with limited context.

claims.paraphrase: Overlapping dialogue is said to dictate a scene's energy and rhythm.
claims.uncertainty: A static graphic confirms the topic but not audible overlap.

claims.paraphrase: Interjections force Mark to overpower several speakers, escalating the deposition exchange.
claims.uncertainty: Power and organic escalation are analysis; the screenplay/film line is visibly aligned.

claims.paraphrase: Misunderstanding is described as a way to reveal exposition without a separate explanation speech.
claims.uncertainty: Course-style generalization.

claims.paraphrase: Different trains of thought challenge the audience to keep up and pull attention into the scene.
claims.uncertainty: Audience effect requires testing.

claims.paraphrase: The opening's China, SAT and final-club misalignments encode Mark's motivation, Erica's patience and exposition while conversation continues.
claims.uncertainty: The page and video show matching lines; characterization is interpretation.

claims.paraphrase: Later misunderstandings are used to characterize Mark's communication difficulty and fragile ego.
claims.uncertainty: Critical reading, not a clinical claim.

claims.paraphrase: The analysis argues that a long dialogue scene remains understandable because recurring misalignments are punctuated by decisive beats.
claims.uncertainty: The claimed page count and effect depend on draft and viewer.

claims.paraphrase: The video's second layer is structure: scenes and jumps can perform several story functions beyond dialogue.
claims.uncertainty: Organizing claim.

claims.paraphrase: The first linear screenplay movement gives way to deposition flash-forwards that add exposition, emotional framing and reactions to past events.
claims.uncertainty: Page and CUT anchors are visible; full sequence needs moving evidence.

claims.paraphrase: Nonlinear order is said to shift the dramatic question from what happens to how a friendship deteriorates.
claims.uncertainty: Known real events may also contribute to the what-to-how shift.

claims.paraphrase: An interview excerpt attributes Fincher's revisions to searching for the dramatic thought beneath each word.
claims.uncertainty: Edited interview context; not independent evidence of every revision.

claims.paraphrase: Removing repeated thesis language is described as desorking: preserving function while reducing overt repetition.
claims.uncertainty: Could also reflect runtime or draft-version differences.

claims.paraphrase: Fincher's cutting is contrasted with walk-and-talk staging as a different way to make dense words cinematic.
claims.uncertainty: Selected comparison, not a universal directing rule.

claims.paraphrase: A rain deposition passage is described as two script pages translated into many angles and cuts.
claims.uncertainty: A visible 16-cell graphic does not independently prove 16 angles or 33 cuts; those numbers remain video claims.

claims.paraphrase: Fast speech, multiple thought lines and verbal hesitations create performance difficulty; Jesse Eisenberg is said to naturalize the hesitations.
claims.uncertainty: Performance interpretation; a still can show beat notation but not spoken rhythm.

claims.paraphrase: The synthesis argues that stylized dialogue depends on actors, director and editor making it playable and cinematic.
claims.uncertainty: Broad collaboration thesis, not a causal allocation formula.
